Qasim Lodhi For Union City Councilmember · District 4
Union City City Council · District 4 · November 3, 2026
# A Fresh Perspective. Passion for Improvement.
Software Engineer. MBA. Father. Community Organizer.
Donate Join the Campaign
## Putting City Resources to Work for You!
Too often, residents have to work too hard to be heard, understand what City Hall is doing, or get a clear answer about a local concern. I want to make participation easier and decisions more transparent for the people that City Council serves.
As a software engineer and a father, I have built my career and my life around solving practical problems, improving systems, and preparing for the future. I will bring that same discipline to City Hall, so our government works more effectively for residents and helps create a safer, more prosperous future for every child in our community.
Proven technology can make local government more accessible, responsive, and transparent. Secure, practical tools can help residents find information, share feedback, track requests, and receive timely updates—while keeping people, judgment, and accountability at the center of every decision.
I have lived in the Bay Area since 2008 and proudly called Union City home since 2021. I love the diversity, energy, and promise of our community—and I believe residents deserve a local government that listens, communicates clearly, and delivers results. I am running for City Council to bring practical problem-solving, an open door, and decisive action to City Hall. Together, we can close the distance between residents and their government and build a Union City that works better for everyone.
Here are practical ways to make City Hall easier to use, more responsive, and more accountable:
- a simple online dashboard that tracks city projects, spending, and service requests;
- smart tools that group recurring requests by neighborhood and topic, route them to the right city department, and publish status updates so concerns do not disappear into a backlog;
- multilingual, two-way communication notifications that keep residents informed about public meetings, emergencies, and issues affecting their neighborhoods;
- more frequent District Dialog meetings;
- clear follow-up timelines so residents know who is responsible and when to expect action;
- a multilingual resident-feedback portal, available by web and mobile, that makes it easy to submit ideas, report concerns, and support priorities raised by neighbors;
- public dashboards and short surveys that let residents see which ideas have the strongest community support, along with participatory budgeting tools that give people a direct voice in how designated city funds are spent.
These are achievable steps that can make City Hall easier to navigate, expand participation, and turn community feedback into measurable results.
This is bigger than adopting a few new tools. A tech-forward, people-first City Council would begin with residents’ needs, advance strong ideas based on clear evidence and community priorities, and give people fast, comprehensive ways to see how the Council is performing, what progress is being made, and where decisions stand. With easier access to results, proposals, and opportunities to participate, residents can contribute their ideas earlier, help shape how solutions are adopted, and have a stronger voice in the decisions that affect them. The goal is straightforward: greater transparency, more meaningful participation, quicker answers, and more problems solved for the people of Union City!
### Your Priorities. My Commitment.
### Participation and Transparency
Make sure taxpayers receive real value from every city dollar by improving public facilities, modernizing city systems, and making government performance easy to understand. I will support secure, user-friendly tools that give residents quick access to city spending, project updates, service results, and Council decisions. I will also expand opportunities for community feedback and use enhanced resident satisfaction surveys to identify priorities, measure progress, and keep City Hall accountable to the people it serves.
### Strengthen Public Safety and Neighborhood Security
Increase visible, community-focused patrols in neighborhoods, parks, and commercial areas so residents see a responsive public-safety presence, concerns are addressed sooner, and stronger relationships are built between officers and the people they serve.
Modernize street lighting with energy-efficient LED fixtures, smart controls, motion sensing where appropriate, and solar-powered options where practical. Better, more reliable lighting can improve visibility for pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers; make parks, sidewalks, and transit stops more welcoming after dark; and help deter crime. An efficient system can also lower electricity costs, reduce outages, and require fewer bulb replacements and service visits—freeing city resources over the next five to ten years for other neighborhood priorities.
### Expand Recreation and Family Entertainment
Invest in modern parks, well-maintained sports fields, and welcoming community centers. Expand youth programs, community events, and family-friendly entertainment so residents of all ages have more opportunities to gather, stay active, and enjoy their city without having to travel elsewhere.
### Support Local Businesses and Grow Our Economy
Help local entrepreneurs start, grow, and succeed by making city processes easier to navigate and attracting new employers, restaurants, shops, and services that meet residents’ needs. A stronger local economy can create jobs, keep more spending in Union City, and expand the tax base without placing a greater burden on homeowners.
### Revitalize Union City’s Public Spaces
Refresh aging streetscapes, gateways, commercial corridors, and other public spaces with thoughtful landscaping, cleaner surroundings, updated signage, and coordinated improvements. A more attractive and welcoming city can strengthen neighborhood pride, encourage local investment, and create places residents are proud to call home.
## Union City by the Numbers
- −6.9% Population decline Young families are moving out. Citywide population fell from 70,143 in April 2020 to 65,282 in July 2025. Residents under 18 fell from 19% in the 2020 Census to 17% in 2020–2024 estimates. U.S. Census Bureau · QuickFacts
- 351 Reported vehicle thefts Stronger prevention. Safer neighborhoods. Motor-vehicle theft offenses citywide in 2025; separate from car break-ins. Union City Police · 2025 report, p. 31
- 1,526 Reported serious crimes Build on progress. Keep improving safety. Citywide in 2025; down 30% from 2024 in UCPD’s comparison. Covers eight serious-crime categories. Union City Police · 2025 report, pp. 31–32
- $2,713 Median monthly gross rent Citywide Census estimate for 2020–2024; includes rent and utilities. U.S. Census Bureau · 2020–2024
- 32 min Average one-way commute For Union City workers, 2020–2024. Census mean: 31.9 minutes, rounded to 32. U.S. Census Bureau · 2020–2024
